items.text: Proof that the diagonal is an immersion
$S$ affine; $X=\bigcup X_i$ affine; $X\times_S X=\bigcup X_i\times_S X_j$; the inverse image of $X_i\times_S X_j$ under $\Delta$ is $X_i\cap X_j=Z$.
Z\xrightarrow{\ \Delta\ }Z\times_S Z\hookrightarrow X_i\times_S X_j\qquad(\text{second arrow an open immersion})
Cover $Z\subset X'$ (affine) by opens $X'_f$: the intersection $X'_f\cap X'_g=X'_{fg}$ is affine.
Z=\operatorname{Spec}B\ \text{over}\ \operatorname{Spec}A:\qquad B\otimes_A B\to B,\ \ x\otimes y\mapsto xy\ \text{surjective: a closed immersion}
Hence: $g\circ f$ an immersion $\Rightarrow$ $f$ an immersion; conversely (with $\mathrm{pr}_1\circ\Delta=\mathrm{id}$) this implies diagonals are in the class.
Diagonals are in the class for monomorphisms, locally of finite type, immersions; not for affine, quasi-compact, finite type, locally of finite presentation, open or closed immersions.
Immersions and finite presentation
An immersion $X=V(\mathcal J)\subset U\subset Y$ is locally of finite presentation $\iff$ $\mathcal J$ is of finite type.
Lemma. If $f$ is locally of finite type, the diagonal $\Delta_f$ is locally of finite presentation.
Reduce to affine: $B$ an $A$-algebra of finite type, $I=\ker(B\otimes_A B\to B)$ is of finite type.
B=A[b_i]:\qquad I=\bigl(\,b_i\otimes1-1\otimes b_i\,\bigr)_i
Two homomorphisms $B\rightrightarrows C$ agreeing on the generators coincide.
Separated morphisms
$f\colon X\to S$ separated iff the diagonal $\Delta_f\colon X\to X\times_S X$ (already an immersion) is a closed immersion, i.e. $\Delta_f(X)$ is closed.

Equivalently: for every base change, every section of $X'\to S'$ is a closed immersion; for every $S$-morphism $Y\to X$ the graph is closed; for all $u,v\colon Y\rightrightarrows X$ over $S$, $\ker(u,v)$ is a closed subscheme of $Y$.
Prolongation principle of identities
$Y$ reduced over $S$, $u,v\colon Y\to X$ two $S$-morphisms, $X$ separated over $S$.
u|_U=v|_U\ \text{for }U\subset Y\ \text{open dense}\ \Longrightarrow\ u=v
Proof: the coincidence scheme $\ker(u,v)$ is a closed subscheme of $Y$ containing the dense $U$, so equal to $Y$ as a set; $Y$ reduced gives equality as schemes.
\text{same with }i\colon U\to Y,\ i(U)\ \text{dense},\ \ u\circ i=v\circ i\ \Rightarrow\ u=v
A surjective immersion is a closed immersion with nil ideal $\mathcal J$; into a reduced scheme it is an isomorphism.
The prolongation principle implies separated (converse). Monomorphisms are separated (their diagonal is an isomorphism); in particular immersions.
$X$ separated over $S$ and $X\to Y$ an $S$-morphism $\Rightarrow$ $X$ separated over $Y$. Diagonals are separated.
Absolute: $X$ separated if separated over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$. Affine schemes: $A\otimes A\to A$ surjective, so separated.
$S$ separated: $X$ separated over $S$ $\iff$ $X$ separated (absolutely).
Consequences of separatedness
$S$ separated, $X$ affine $\Rightarrow$ $f\colon X\to S$ is affine; equivalently, $X,Y$ affine over $S$ $\Rightarrow$ $X\times_S Y$ affine.
\begin{CD} X\times_S Y @>>> S\\ @VVV @VV{\Delta}V\\ X\times Y @>>> S\times S \end{CD}
$X\times Y$ affine, $\Delta$ a closed immersion hence affine, so $X\times_S Y\to X\times Y$ is affine.
Corollary. In a separated scheme the intersection of two affine opens is affine.
Counterexample: the line with doubled origin
$X'=X''=\mathbf E^1_S$; glue along $X'^*=X''^*$ (complement of the zero section) by the identity.
Not separated: $u,v\colon\mathbf E^1\rightrightarrows X$ (the two inclusions) agree on $Z^*$, dense, but $u\neq v$.
\Delta^{-1}(X_i\times_S X_j)=X_i\cap X_j;\qquad X_1\cap X_2=Z^*\to Z\times_S Z=\mathbf E^2_S
Z^*\hookrightarrow Z\xrightarrow{\ \Delta\ }Z\times_S Z
$\Delta$ is affine ($Z^*$ and $Z$ affine over $S$) but not closed ($Z^*\to Z$ has dense, non-closed image): affine diagonal does not give separated.
